Privacy Policy

What This Site Collects (And What It Doesn't)

Last updated 2026. Written in plain language on purpose, the same way this whole page argues a privacy policy should be.

USES

This site uses basic, aggregate web analytics: which pages get visited, roughly how people found them (referrer), and general device or browser type. It's used only to understand what's useful on this page and what isn't.

NOT

No accounts, no logins, no personal profiles are built. Nothing is sold to anyone. No third-party advertising trackers are embedded on this page.

STORAGE

Your dark mode preference and quiz progress live in your browser's local storage. They're never sent to a server; they just stay on your device so the setting sticks the next time you visit.

CONTACT

Questions about this page or its data practices can go through creativepea.com.

This site is a free educational project, not a business collecting data for profit. This policy will stay this short because there genuinely isn't more to disclose. If that ever changes, this page changes with it.

F-Pattern Reading

The coral shape is a heatmap, not a decoration. Eyes hit the full top line first, then a shorter second pass, then trail down the left edge scanning for anything worth stopping for. Everything outside that shape gets skimmed or skipped.

What to do with this: put your strongest words at the start of the first two lines and down the left edge. Don't bury your point in the middle of a paragraph.

Z-Pattern for Landing Pages

① Logo
② Sign Up
④ Learn More
③ Get Started

On pages with more visuals than text, like most landing pages, eyes don't scan line by line. They jump corner to corner: top-left, across to top-right, diagonally down to bottom-left, then across to bottom-right, tracing a Z.

What to do with this: put your logo top-left, your account/sign-up link top-right, and your main call-to-action bottom-right, right where the Z ends.

The 8pt Grid System

Card Title

16px below the icon, 16px below this line, 16px of padding all around.

Action

Every dot in the grid above is 8px apart. The card's padding, the gap under the icon, and the gap under this paragraph are all exactly 16px, which is 2 dots. Nothing here was placed by eye.

What to do with this: before you type a random padding value, ask whether 8, 16, 24, or 32 already does the job. It almost always does.

Glassmorphism Explained

This card uses glassmorphism

Glassmorphism is that frosted-glass effect you see everywhere now (thanks, Apple). It uses backdrop-filter: blur() to blur whatever is behind an element.

The CSS magic

.glass {
  background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.1);
  backdrop-filter: blur(10px);
  -webkit-backdrop-filter: blur(10px);
  border: 1px solid rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.2);
  border-radius: 12px;
}

Why it works: transparency + blur creates visual hierarchy without blocking content.

When to use: modals, navigation overlays, tooltips.

Browser support: works in all modern browsers. Safari needs -webkit-backdrop-filter.

Navigation, Six Ways

Top Nav

Logo left, links right. The default for a reason: predictable, always visible.

Hamburger Menu

Collapses everything behind one icon. Saves space, costs a tap. Mostly a mobile pattern now.

Sidebar Nav

Vertical, persistent. Common for dashboards and docs where there are too many sections for a top bar.

Mega Menu

A dropdown that opens into a full grid of links. For sites with deep catalogs: retailers, big docs sites.

Bottom Tab Bar

Icons and short labels, pinned to the bottom. The standard for mobile apps, thumb-reachable.

›
›

Breadcrumbs

A trail, not a menu. Shows where you are in a hierarchy. Pairs with, doesn't replace, primary nav.

Same job, six different shapes.

Hero Sections, Five Ways

Text-Only, Centered

Just a headline, a line of support copy, and a button. Fast to build, fast to load, hard to get wrong.

Split Hero

Copy on one side, a product shot or illustration on the other. Shows and tells at the same time.

Full-Bleed Background

A photo or video fills the whole section, text sits on top with an overlay for contrast. High impact, needs a real image.

Product Screenshot

A short pitch above an actual screenshot of the product. Common for SaaS: it proves the thing is real.

Video Background

Looping, muted, autoplaying footage behind the headline. Heavy to load, needs a reduced-motion fallback.

Pick the one your content can actually support.

Three Ways to Handle the Fold

The One-Screen Pitch

Everything essential (what it is, why it matters, what to click) fits before the dashed line. Nothing below is required reading.

The Teaser Peek

A sliver of the next section is deliberately visible past the fold. It signals "there's more" without a scroll indicator.

↓

The Explicit Scroll Cue

An arrow, chevron, or "scroll to explore" label removes any doubt that there's more content below.

All three work. Silence about it is the only wrong answer.

Content Sections, Five Ways

Card Grid

Equal-weight items in a repeating grid. Features, team members, blog posts: anything that's a list of peers.

Zig-Zag Rows

Image and text alternate sides row to row. Slower to scan than a grid, better for telling a sequence of points.

Tabs

One panel visible at a time behind a row of switches. Keeps a busy page short at the cost of hiding content.

List / Table

Rows of structured data. Pricing comparisons, changelogs, specs: anything better scanned than read.

Carousel

One item centered and emphasized, neighbors peeking at the edges. Good for testimonials, risky for anything important.

The shape should fit the content, not the other way around.

Footers, Four Ways

Minimal

A few links and a copyright line. Right for small sites with nothing else that needs saying.

Mega Footer

A full sitemap in columns. Common on large sites where the footer doubles as secondary navigation and SEO.

Newsletter Footer

An email field and a button, front and center. The footer as one last chance to capture the visitor.

App-Download Footer

Store badges instead of links. For products where the real destination is a mobile app, not more web pages.

Same last impression, different jobs.

Contrast Checker

Real WCAG math, calculated in your browser as you type. No values are sent anywhere.

The quick fox jumps.

Body text at a normal reading size.

21.00 : 1
AA Normal Text AA Large Text AAA Normal Text AAA Large Text

Normal text needs 4.5:1 (AA) or 7:1 (AAA). Large text (18px+, or 14px+ bold) and UI borders need 3:1 (AA) or 4.5:1 (AAA).
